articles.title_orig: Israeli ‘direct hit ‘on Doctors Without Borders Gaza clinic kills 2 staff
articles.title_zh: Israeli ‘direct hit ‘on Doctors Without Borders Gaza clinic kills 2 staff
articles.content_orig:
Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.
It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the killings bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.
The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.
It called for those responsible to be held accountable.
In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.
World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.
“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.
The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.
Saul Takahashi, a former deputy head of office of the United Nations high commissioner for human rights in occupied Palestine, said “there is no way” that the attack was an isolated event.
“It’s part and parcel of the entire campaign of genocide,” he told Al Jazeera. “From the get-go, from the very beginning, the Israelis announced that they were going to prohibit any kind of humanitarian, or any other kind of aid, from entering Gaza; essentially that they were using starvation and the prohibition of humanitarian aid as a weapon in their campaign of genocide,” said Takahashi.
Israel’s forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers since the start of its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.
Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.
Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.
Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.
The strike came despite a “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated.
Israeli attacks during this period have killed at least 1,705 people, bringing the overall death toll in the war to at least 74,772, according to the Health Ministry in Gaza.

articles.title_orig: Russia charges air force deputy chief with taking large bribe
articles.title_zh: Russia charges air force deputy chief with taking large bribe
articles.content_orig:
Russia has arrested Aerospace Forces (VKS) Deputy Commander in Chief Yuri Grekhov on charges of accepting a particularly large bribe, the latest in a series of corruption cases against senior military figures since the country changed its defence minister in 2024.
Grekhov, 64, oversaw procurement of aircraft, munitions, missiles and air defence systems. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to 15 years under Russian law.
Grekhov has been on the EU sanctions list since 2022, when Brussels deemed him responsible for Russian strikes on military and civilian sites after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A career military officer since 1979, Grekhov became deputy commander in chief under Alexander Chaiko in 2021, after commanding the air and missile defence forces from 2018 to 2021.
Unlike most of the other officials detained in recent cases, Grekhov is a serving officer, making him one of the most senior figures to come under investigation while still in post.
The VKS controls Russia's military aviation, space operations and strategic missile defence, and has played a central role in strikes on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the war.
At least a dozen senior ministry employees and generals have been detained or become criminal suspects since Andrei Belousov replaced the dismissed Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.
Belousov, an economist with no military background, was appointed with an explicit mandate to impose financial discipline on the defence ministry in what Moscow said was part of a crackdown on corruption within military ranks.
The most prominent case was the arrest of former Deputy Defence Minister Timur Ivanov in April 2024.
A close associate of Shoigu for more than a decade, Ivanov was convicted of taking a particularly large bribe in Defence Ministry contracting work, embezzlement and money laundering. He was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony and fined 100 million roubles (€1 million).
Former first deputy defence minister Ruslan Tsalikov was detained in March 2026 on charges of creating a criminal organisation, embezzlement and laundering budget funds. In November he received 10 years in a high-security penal colony and a fine of 500 million roubles (€5 million).
Others detained for bribery and embezzlement include former Deputy Chief of the General Staff Vadim Shamarin, sentenced to seven years, former head of the Defence Ministry's Main Personnel Directorate Yuri Kuznetsov, sentenced to 12 years, and former Deputy Defence Ministers Dmitry Bulgakov and Pavel Popov.
Several Western governments have assessed that the prosecutions also serve to selectively remove officials who have fallen out of favour with the Kremlin.
The pattern of cases allows Moscow to present itself as enforcing accountability while using criminal charges as a tool of internal political control.

articles.title_orig: Don’t Let China Hawks Exploit the Nvidia Scandal
articles.title_zh: Don’t Let China Hawks Exploit the Nvidia Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Amid the flurry of commentary over Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s “gone today, here tomorrow” act, there is one question that remains undiscussed: Has U.S. policy toward China succeeded in its aims of maintaining American preeminence and security?
The overwhelming reaction to Huang’s reinstatement has been bipartisan outrage at U.S. President Donald Trump’s interference in a private company, coupled with demands for stricter enforcement of U.S. export controls on the sale of Nvidia’s chips to China. As Sen. Tom Cotton said , “I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access”.
That sentiment is widely shared. But should it be?
There was a point sometime in the mid-2010s when U.S. policy shifted decisively from engaging China to containing it. This began during U.S. President Barack Obama’s second term, and then it accelerated with the first tariff war and the campaign against Huawei during the first season of the Trump show. It was cemented as consensus policy during the U.S. President Joe Biden’s interregnum and has been maintained during the second season of Trump.
This shift was driven by a growing consensus that engagement had failed. China’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 was supposed to make it more democratic and open. It did not. China under President Xi Jinping instead turned away from political reforms, silencing any hint of opposition to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Internationally, Beijing adopted a more confrontational stance toward the United States while continuing to steal American intellectual property.
In this context, Washington embraced export controls on high-end technology that could enhance the Chinese military or give Chinese companies an edge in the race for preeminence in artificial intelligence. But instead of meaningfully containing or slowing China, these export controls have only succeeded in raising tensions and increasing the potential of a future war.
By most informed accounts , the restrictions in place since 2022 have delayed or impaired the ability of Chinese companies to build AI frontier models on the scale, scope, and speed of Anthropic or OpenAI. The restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment sales to China have also created supply constraints that have pressured the Chinese military.
As a result, however, China has become far more self-reliant and aggressively built out its own domestic chip design and manufacturing. Though these domestic efforts lag behind the United States, Nvidia, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company by months or even a few years, this has not prevented dramatic breakthroughs such as the unveiling of China’s AI model DeepSeek.
What’s more, China has managed to evade export controls and obtain high-end chips, either through third parties and other countries in Southeast Asia or through good old-fashioned theft and copying. If Nvidia knowingly and purposely evaded those controls with the acquiescence of some in the Trump administration, that remains a profound scandal. But the reality is that even without this kind of corruption, sanctions have consistently failed to prevent countries from accessing things that are available worldwide, even highly controlled military equipment. A country as large and as intertwined with the global economy as China simply cannot be cut off for long.
By trying to control China’s chip access and only partly succeeding, Washington has pushed Beijing into a more unequivocally hostile stance. The CCP and Xi perceived, rightly, that the United States had no intention of allowing its peaceful rise and concluded that confrontation was inevitable.
Especially in the past two years, Washington also began to cut off China’s access to aspects of the domestic U.S. market. The Trump administration has blocked Chinese attempts to purchase U.S. companies and prevented thousands of Chinese students from studying at American universities. Students and investments both made China more dependent on and integrated with the United States.
But many Americans, drawing the wrong lessons from the brief period of Japanese ascendency in the late 1980s, saw these developments as a sign of American weakness, not strength. Japan’s investment in Rockefeller Center and Pebble Beach actually bound the country more closely to the United States and in the process demonstrated how attractive and singular U.S. properties and capital markets were (and are). Instead of recognizing this, policymakers simply carried their aversion to foreign investment over to China.
In the past year, both the Trump administration and Xi seem to have established what was termed “mutually assured disruption”. China can withhold rare-earth exports that are vital to tech companies everywhere, while Washington can use trade restrictions to squeeze the China export machine. The result has been a period of relative calm in U.S.-China tensions.
Now, with the Nvidia drama, that modus vivendi is in question on Capitol Hill. Congress sees the complicity of the White House as a political opening that it can exploit to double down on its preferred strategy of strangling Chinese technological growth.
But the calls for greater export controls and more scrutiny of trade will not make the United States economically or militarily more secure. They will instead push China ever deeper into its adversarial stance. In this new climate, any vestiges of bilateral engagement will be harder to sustain, aggravating the relationship that will determine the stability of the global system over the next decades.
There is still time to pursue a better policy. From the outset, Washington should have loosened controls on high-end chip exports, which could have helped ease Xi and the CCP’s iron grip on China and soothe bilateral tensions over time. The refrain that the United States can’t afford to let China win the race for artificial general intelligence is grounded in the same fallacy that any country could contain such a technology and that there is some magical first-mover advantage. There certainly wasn’t with any prior technology, nuclear weapons included.
A more sensible and open policy on chip exports remains the best path going forward. Congress can still pursue it, even as it seeks to hold Trump accountable for any corrupt acts—and Huang for any mistakes he may have made. Nvidia’s scandals do not prove that engagement was wrong and should not preclude the United States and China from developing a more cooperative relationship. Global peace should not be sacrificed on account of Huang’s actions, or Trump’s.
Zachary Karabell is the author of the Edgy Optimist Substack and an opinion contributor at the Washington Post.

articles.title_orig: Far-Right Vigilantes Have Inflamed France’s Unrest, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Far-Right Vigilantes Have Inflamed France’s Unrest, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.
This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.
President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.
That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.
The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.
So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?
It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.
My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.
You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.
French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).
Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.
Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.
As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.
Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.
"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.
"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."
"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."
These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.
They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.
Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.
I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.
They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.
"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."
How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?
They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.
French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.
Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.
Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.
He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.
"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.
"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."
I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?
As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.
"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."
When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.
Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.
There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.
While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?
All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?
It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?
"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."
"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage an

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Embrace of Xi and Huang Stun China Critics in Washington
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Embrace of Xi and Huang Stun China Critics in Washington
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.
She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Iran hitting same ships twice to deter traffic from Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Iran hitting same ships twice to deter traffic from Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Iranian forces said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest in a string of incidents in the waterway, as the U.S. escalates sanctions aimed at cutting off Tehran's financial lifelines.
In a statement carried by state news agency IRNA, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three "offending" oil tankers "suffered a severe explosion and fire after hitting naval mines" in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guards said one tanker was near the southern coast and two were in the eastern part of the strait. All three were under extensive U.S. military air cover and escort that failed to prevent the explosions.
"U.S. military cover and escort will not replace compliance with maritime regulations and instructions from the IRGC Navy Traffic Control Center," the statement said.
Iranian forces have repeatedly warned commercial vessels that only the northern shipping lane has been approved by Tehran for safe passage, while attacking or threatening ships that use alternative routes near Oman.
The U.S. added a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, to the Gulf last week, joining two other carriers in the fleet enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The tanker incidents came after the U.S. Treasury on Monday announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of what it called "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks."
Iran's economy has come under growing pressure as Washington expanded sanctions under its so-called "Operation Economic Outcast" since August, aimed at crippling financial networks behind the country's oil revenue.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in Monday's statement, described Iran's economy as "underwater," saying its shadow banking system was "the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime."
The conflict also appears to have extended to cyberspace, with Washington investigating Iran as a primary suspect behind dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday .
As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals and other potentially hazardous cargoes were believed to have been targeted, while some received warnings and bomb threats, the Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter.
U.S. authorities were also examining Russia as another possible culprit, according to the report, which described the widening attacks and occasional ransom messages as part of Iran's efforts to stoke fear among shipowners and further disrupt energy flows.
The foreign ministries of Iran and Russia did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
The conflict, triggered by the U.S. and Israeli strikes in late February, has seen Tehran close the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. impose a blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf, squeezing energy shipments through one of the world's most critical shipping conduits.
Oil futures inched lower Tuesday as investors looked past continued attacks on tankers to price in rising supplies from the region. On Tuesday, international benchmark Brent futures dipped to $89.2 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell to $80.1 per barrel, down from the October high of nearly $105 per barrel.
Pressure on oil prices has eased as regional crude supply recovered and Russian exports rebounded, loosening supply constraints ahead of winter, said Gregory Brew, senior analyst for Iran and energy at Eurasia Group.
Russian refined-product exports recovered in November, with diesel shipments rising back to 400,000 barrels per day, Brew said. But "intensifying Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz could reverse that trend," he added, estimating Brent would remain in the lower half of an $80-100-per-barrel range.

articles.title_orig: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts warn
articles.title_zh: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts warn
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Rumours have begun to suggest that one of the most fundamental technologies that secures the modern internet could have been undone by AI .
In recent days, computer scientists and AI experts have begun to suggest that frontier artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic may have made discoveries that are so powerful that they could undermine security. Many suggest that the public has not heard about it precisely because those discoveries are so powerful – because letting the world know would also mean allowing the discovery to be used.
The fears relate to encryption , the technology that is used to scramble messages so that they cannot be intercepted as they move across the internet. That would not only threaten our private conversations – though it would do that – but all of the other private information that is sent over the web, from banking transactions to other personal information.
If encryption were to be broken, then theoretically all of our private data could be stolen as it is transmitted, and from there people would be able to break into any system that relied on the technology. As such, a threat to modern encryption is a threat to the very way the internet works.
The rumours relate specifically to RSA, a particular tool that is used in that encryption process. It works by using prime numbers to scramble up messages in a way that is practically impossible to guess, but trivially easy to work out if you have those prime numbers – making sure that messages can be read by anyone who has the key, but not by anybody else.
Since it was developed in the 1970s, that system has held strong, and there have been no reports of sufficiently advanced systems having been broken into. But for years computer scientists have worried that it could eventually be broken – and rumours are now suggesting that it has.
In recent days, a host of social media posts have suggested that there are rumours coming from those leading AI labs that suggest they have reached a breakthrough that would undermine cryptography. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson, a leading computer scientist, for instance wrote an expletive-laden blog post in which he suggested that he was “virtually certain” that AI companies were hiding “bombshells” that would “break currently deployed cryptosystems”.
The concerns have become so widespread and substantial that they have been put to many of the most powerful people in the world. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey was for instance asked this week whether he was aware of AI systems that are capable of breaking encryption – and while he did not say that they had, he noted that the companies say that they are on “the exponential part of the development curve”.
Ben Spencer, the shadow minister for AI, has also raised the question in parliament. He wrote to Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy to ask “what assessment she has made of the potential impact of the use of Al to find weaknesses in cryptographic algorithms on the security of government systems”.
The rumours are odd in that they relate, partly, specifically to what AI companies have not done. In recent weeks, both OpenAI and Anthropic have published papers on a huge range of unsolved mathematical problems, but very few of them have had any connection with encryption or with security more generally.
That may simply be a coincidence, or it may reflect the fact that those problems are either harder to solve or so dangerous that the companies have opted not to pursue them. But, some suggest, it could be an indication that they have made progress on these questions that is sufficiently dangerous that it should not be put out into the world.
Given that the news – if there is any – is being kept secret, however, it is hard to know exactly how much damage it would do to the internet. Even if the discoveries are as powerful as some have suggested, for instance, it does not necessarily mean that it would undermine all cryptography, just some specific ways of building it.
The effect of any such breakthrough might be limited by the fact that many of the world’s leading computing companies and experts have already been worrying about the reliability of cryptography for some time. While the threat from AI might be relatively new, researchers have been warning for years about the danger of a “quantum apocalypse” – the concern that new, more powerful quantum computers could themselves be able to crack the problems that currently power encryption .
That is still some way off: quantum computers are still in their infancy, and are far from being able to do the kind of work that would be needed to pose a threat to encryption. But security experts have been upgrading their systems nonetheless, to ensure that they are ready, and many of the most important systems have already moved to new and more secure ways of protecting their data.
Part of that is an effort to ensure that those systems are ready for whatever challenges might arrive in the future. But part of it is about the present, and a warning for anyone concerned about the danger that AI might pose: experts warn about the possibility of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, in which hackers might steal data now and then break into it when the capabilities to do so are available.
Those worries and others like them have led to a focus on “cryptographic agility”, or the idea that systems should be built with the ability to switch between different kinds of cryptography as the need to do so arises. That means that systems should not be so vulnerable to attack from the kinds of breakthroughs rumoured to have happened at the AI companies – not because they are necessarily protected from them, but because they are able to move to a different and safer kind of protection when those challenges come up.
For now, neither Anthropic nor OpenAI have publicly given any information about their work on encryption, including whether they have made any such breakthrough, or even whether they are working on them. While that might be frustrating and worrying to the computing experts who are speculating that they might be hiding dangerous breakthroughs, it might also help keep the world safer – since the really dangerous thing is not whether any such new discovery has been made, but whether people know about it, and are able to exploit it.

articles.title_orig: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash on rescue mission
articles.title_zh: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash on rescue mission
articles.content_orig:
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.
Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.
Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine , according to the United Nations.

If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June , you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.
The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount , is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.
Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model , the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display , or one of the M6-powered machines . A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

articles.title_orig: Two planes clip wings at Reagan National Airport
articles.title_zh: Two planes clip wings at Reagan National Airport
articles.content_orig:
Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday.
One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.
Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.
The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.
"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.
Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.
The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.
A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.
The passenger added that the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and he heard gasps inside the cabin. He described the moment as "tense", but that nobody seemed to be hurt.
As he looked out the window, he saw a piece of the aircraft on the ground. It looked like the "tip of the wing", he said, describing how the other aircraft's wing  was overlapping his plane's wing.
The BBC has contacted American Airlines about reports of the broken wingtip.
As they taxied back to the gate, the passenger said he saw a truck pick up the piece that had fallen.
The fact that this isn't the first incident at this airport was "definitely scary", the passenger said.
Last year, there was a deadly mid-air collision between another American Airlines flight and a military helicopter at Reagan National.
The 64 people on the passenger plane and three US Army members on the Black Hawk helicopter all died in the crash.
The aircraft, en route to land at the DC airport after leaving from Wichita, Kansas, was sent careening into the Potomac River upon impact with the military helicopter.
It was later determined that the helicopter was receiving faulty altitude data, causing it to fly higher than intended.
Reagan National Airport is the smaller of the two DC-area airports and caters mostly  to domestic flights.
It sits right near the sprawl of the US capital, the White House and the Pentagon.
Earlier this week, the US Army said it planned to resume helicopter test flights near Reagan airport, according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. The flights were paused following last year's incident.
BBC has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
articles.content_orig:
That GTA 6 was going to be a hit was never in doubt, and the glowing reviews that arrived as the copies finally unlocked on the 18th ensured it. The scale of its success still managed to surprise, though: 32.5 million copies and revenue of $3.79b on the first day , surpassing all expectations. Analysts talking to GamesIndustry.biz have commended the game's unprecedented attach rate, but say that with the console install base limited, the currently-unconfirmed PC release is the chief scale opportunity.
Joost van Dreunen - who says the release was "unlike anything else we've seen before" - says his initial projection of $2b after the first weekend "put more weight on the relative sluggishness in overall consumer spending and the recent price increases for both hardware and software," conceding that "clearly GTA 6 didn't suffer any gravitational drag during its launch." Sensor Tower's Karl Kontus, meanwhile, points out that the firm's widely-reported figure of 24.5 million pre-orders only referred to digital pre-orders, while Rockstar's number included day-one sales and physical sell-in; he says the digital pre-order figure ended up at 26M, and holds the firm's estimate was "pretty much spot on".
Sensor Tower now projects 47m units sold by the end of the launch weekend, while Ampere Analysis suggests 40.2m in the same period (albeit on the GMT timezone). All firms have high expectations for year-end: Ampere's Piers Harding-Rolls says that "50 million+ is achievable by the end of the year," van Dreunen expects 50m, and Gareth Sutcliffe of Enders Analysis points to the firm's previously-stated "bull case" range of 50-60m. "I don't think it has hit its entire addressable market yet, especially with the major holidays still ahead of us," says van Dreunen.
"Franchises build momentum over time. Take-Two initially focused on its premium console fanbase, but has clearly reached a much broader audience. Their marketing campaign has focused as much on core gamers as on a more mainstream audience. Take-Two positioned GTA 6 less as a game and more as a blockbuster entertainment event."
For the next level of sales growth, the limit is the number of consoles in the market. "There are about 137 million current-gen consoles in the world, and a quarter of them bought a copy before its release," says van Dreunen. "The rest of this year is about the other three-quarters, and next year is about PC." Kontus calls the attach rate "unprecedented" and Sutcliffe agrees. "It’s clear that GTA 6 will have an attach rate to install base that exceeds any other title ever," he says.
"The key question is if Sony and Xbox have any capability to provide increased and meaningful console supply into the market this quarter, and in Q1. Indications are that they can’t, otherwise they would and definitely should be saying so. The title is clearly going to run up against console install base limitations sooner at this level of run rate."
All eyes are on the PC release, then, and van Dreunen predicts that ultimately the sales will end up at the same level as its predecessor: "It will become a staple for both console and PC gamers, so we can expect a similar number of units sold over its lifetime as GTA 5, translating roughly to 200-250 million for GTA 6."
Sutcliffe suggests an additional wild card: mobile. "If Take Two were to do something ingenious with Apple, such as much broader Apple silicon support beyond Mac, reaching into late generation iPhone and iPad SKUs for example, you would expand the total addressable market into the hundreds of millions of unit range," he says. "We would be in new territory at that point, and also very radical, but given so few were predicting this level of success, the question is how does Take Two get to 100m units otherwise, especially in year 1? It needs more platforms to get there, and getting there quickly will hold its retail price up."
"What I do anticipate is that Take Two will want to expand addressable market faster than the previous release, particularly given this console generation has a reduced net install."
All are united in expecting the PC release to deliver that expansion. While that blowout launch figure exceeded even the highest estimates for the development cost of the game, Take-Two's multi-year investment will have been predicated on a still-larger return, and the current console market has no way of delivering it.
"A decade ago Take Two would have been receiving sunny projections from both Sony and Microsoft on console install growth that have completely fizzled, meanwhile they’re committing to $1b plus in dev spend," says Sutcliffe. "They need to go where the market is as a result, and console has a defined ceiling."

WASHINGTON—United Fidelity Bank, fsb, Evansville, Indiana (United Fidelity) was closed today by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which appointed the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) as receiver. The FDIC entered into an agreement with First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company, Raleigh, North Carolina (First Citizens) to assume substantially all deposits and purchase substantially all assets of United Fidelity.
Depositors of United Fidelity will become depositors of First Citizens, so customers do not need to change their banking relationship and will retain all of their funds and deposit insurance coverage. United Fidelity’s 22 branches in Indiana, Illinois, Florida, Colorado, and the U.S. Virgin Islands will reopen as branches of First Citizens during normal business hours on Saturday at locations that normally operate on Saturdays and on Monday at all other locations. This evening and over the weekend, depositors of United Fidelity can access their money by writing checks or using ATM or debit cards. Checks drawn on United Fidelity will continue to be processed and loan customers should continue to make their payments as usual.
Customers of United Fidelity should continue to use their existing branches until they receive notice from First Citizens that it has completed systems changes to allow First Citizens’ branch offices to process these accounts as well.
Customers with questions about the First Citizens acquisition of United Fidelity may call the FDIC toll-free at 1-866-431-1725 . The FDIC’s Call Center will be open this evening until 8 p.m. Central Time (CT); on Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. CT; on Sunday from noon to 4:00 p.m. CT; on Monday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. CT; and thereafter from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. CT. Interested parties may also visit the FDIC’s website for further information.
As of September 30, 2026, United Fidelity had approximately $5.9 billion in total assets and $5.4 billion in total deposits.  The FDIC estimates that the cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) related to the failure of United Fidelity will be $1.83 billion.

articles.title_orig: The High Political Cost of Trump’s Loyalty to Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: The High Political Cost of Trump’s Loyalty to Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
In a tumultuous three weeks, Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO following revelations of his affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and at least one Nvidia employee. At the time, the company’s board chair said it did not intend to reinstate him, and Huang remained without an employer for 11 days. Then, the White House intervened.
President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other senior officials spent this past weekend lobbying on Huang’s behalf, per the Wall Street Journal, and by Monday, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate him as CEO.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC in a phone call . “And I convinced them.”
Trump told the Journal that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. Trump said he assured the board his administration wouldn’t punish the company for possible violations of export controls or securities laws if it rehired Huang. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is currently probing the company, just as the Times reported that Trump was briefed in 2025 on Huang’s relationship with the woman on intelligence that she was passing information to Beijing, and chose not to act.
But for the president, his intervention to rescue Huang follows a pattern in which the Trump administration has stepped into corporate America’s affairs. The White House has already bought stakes in companies, obtained veto rights over business decisions, and negotiated terms for chip sales to China—the latter of which has been designated a matter of national security .  For some,  Trump’s intervention in Nvidia, however, comes off as the president having a say  in decisions typically left to boards and shareholders—especially since his own portfolio holds Nvidia stock .
In this case, Huang’s importance to Nvidia , whose chips underpin the AI boom, helps explain the White House’s decision, especially for a president who keeps a close eye on the stock market and who has outlined AI as a national priority.
“You can’t really say Nvidia without Jensen is the same as Nvidia with Jensen,” Jeffrey Towson, an AI research analyst and former professor at Peking University’s Guanghua School of Management, told Fortune . “He’s almost a national asset, this guy.”
A growing footprint in the private sector
Reinstating Huang isn’t the first time the Trump administration has struck a deal with Nvidia. It negotiated a deal with the company last year approving its chip exports to China in exchange for 15% of the revenue. In December, it let Nvidia sell its more powerful H200 chips to China in exchange for a 25% cut.
And the administration has taken stakes in other companies. Since January 2025, it has announced 49 investments worth $30.8 billion, according to the Council on Foreign Relations’ Government Deal Tracker. White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton told Fortune the administration’s investments focus on “securing and reshoring America’s critical supply chains.”
“President Trump will continue to work with partners across the public and private sectors to advance solutions that strengthen our economy, secure our supply chains, protect our national security, and put more money back in the pockets of American workers,” Middleton said.
Nvidia also wasn’t the first chipmaker the administration struck deals with. Last year, Trump called for Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan to resign over alleged conflicts of interest with China, but then reversed course after meeting with him. Weeks later, the Trump administration took a 10% stake in Intel . It had also gotten veto rights over certain decisions at U.S. Steel as part of its approval of its $14.1 billion sale to Nippon Steel .
Trump also has a personal stake in Nvidia. Trump’s investment accounts bought between $152,004 and $380,000 worth of Nvidia stock in September, two months before Huang’s resignation, per the president’s financial disclosures released by the Office of Government Ethics on Nov. 19. Nvidia shares closed more than 30% higher the day the board reinstated Huang.
The Trump Organization has said that the accounts are run by independent managers with no input from the president, and the White House previously told Fortune “neither the President nor his family has ever engaged—or will ever engage—in conflicts of interest.”
But the administration’s behavior in Nvidia’s case might have reverberations for the U.S.’s standing in the global economy. Patrick Boyle , a former hedge fund manager and visiting professor of finance at King’s College London and Queen Mary University of London, told Fortune that the lesson the boards of “strategically important” companies are taking away from the Nvidia episode is that they should check in with the White House before making big decisions.
“One of America’s great economic advantages has always been that its companies answer to their shareholders, not to the government,” Boyle said.
Nvidia did not respond to Fortune ’s requests for comment.
Trump’s interventions have drawn some comparisons to China, where the state shapes business policies to align with national interests. But Daniel Schatz, a political scientist who has served as a fellow at the think tank New America’s International Security Program, told Fortune that Trump’s intervention wasn’t “Chinese-style state capitalism,” but is a more personalized form of intervention where the president’s favor “can matter as much as predictable rules.”
“The risk is that a legitimate effort to protect a strategic industry turns into political patronage,” Schatz said.
Towson said China and the U.S. have similar strategic interests in AI and semiconductors, but the mechanisms through which those interests are carried out are different. For the U.S., particularly in the Nvidia case, he said it’s more “chaotic state capitalism” that depends on the stock market, while for China, the focus is on long-term planning.
“The goal of state capitalism is to be able to make longer-term plans outside of market forces,” Towson said. “This seems to be the opposite of that.”

articles.title_orig: Apple is going all in with the iPhone 20 Pro
articles.title_zh: Apple is going all in with the iPhone 20 Pro
articles.content_orig:
Rumours are spreading that Apple is preparing a version of its next flagship model, the iPhone 20 Pro, that uses ceramic material. But no detailed information has been disclosed, and there are views that the chances of an actual launch are low.
On Nov. 26, IT outlet NineToFiveMac reported that Fixed Focus Digital, a Chinese leak account, claimed it had seen ceramic parts to be used in next year’s flagship iPhone. It did not disclose details such as what type of parts they were or how broadly they would be applied.
There are also images shared by Tech Overwatch, but they are renderings showing an expected design rather than photos of an actual product. Some images show a form that applies ceramic material to the back, but it has not been confirmed whether it would be reflected in the actual product.
The rumour may have emerged from confusion with Apple’s existing materials technology. Apple applied Ceramic Shield to the iPhone Air to protect the display and rear glass. Information related to that technology may have been misread as talk of releasing a separate model using ceramic material.
There is also analysis that launching a ceramic model would not be easy from a product strategy perspective. The iPhone 20 Pro itself is already planned as a premium device, and it is known that an entirely new production line would also be needed. In that situation, there is an assessment that Apple is unlikely to add an even more expensive ultra-premium model or test two versions at the same time.
So far, no specific specifications or launch plans have been confirmed beyond the claim that ceramic parts were seen. The render images are also not leaked photos based on an actual product. It is therefore reasonable to view a ceramic iPhone 20 Pro as an early, unverified rumour.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
articles.title_zh: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
articles.content_orig:
Cyberleek has reportedly made good on their promise and released the executable file for the leaked Xbox build of GTA 6 , sparking concern that an unofficial PC port could be around the corner.
The infamous hacker had vowed to release the .exe for the incomplete GTA 6 Xbox build whether the Cyberleek memecoin hit its market cap target or not , and now it is out in the wild, some within the homebrew scene are preparing to take a close look at it.
Cyberleek released the exe with a fresh statement insisting their actions on GTA 6 so far were about “fighting anti-consumerism in the games industry.” Cyberleek also taunts Rockstar parent company Take-Two’s so-far unsuccessful effort to prevent further leaks or, it seems, track down those responsible, saying: “Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving.”
They also pushed back on claims the GTA 6 leaks are about little more than pushing a crypto scheme, insisting that crypto was used to generate funds for a secret project outside of the game. “There is no other way to move funds without names,” Cyberleek said, “and this work requires no names.”
Some are now predicting that AI-assisted recompilation of the leaked Xbox build could result in GTA 6 on PC in just days, with performance improvements over the console version in weeks.
This is of course a nightmare scenario for Take-Two and Sony and Microsoft, which are benefiting greatly from GTA 6 releasing on console only. The console version of GTA 6 targets 30fps across all platforms, although struggles at times to hit that on base PS5, and Xbox Series X and S. As a result, there is huge interest in a potential PC version offering 60fps gameplay.
The release of the Xbox build from this month runs counter to the thought that Cyberleek only had access to an early development build of GTA 6, a feeling that was reinforced not only by the videos that were released in the summer, but by the differences that have emerged following the game’s official launch.
Fans are calling on people not to spend money on Cyberleek, pointing out the leaker cashed out back in August and did again in October. Analysis of cryptocurrency transactions in late August pointed to the GTA 6 leaker cashing out having earnt around $270,000.
IGN had reported on fan skepticism around the alleged leaked gameplay that reportedly showed both Jason and Lucia fully naked . A previous leaked gameplay video allegedly showed a tank spawning into the world, which suggested access to a dev menu of some kind. The leaked videos allegedly showing both Jason and Lucia fully naked also show NPCs failing to react to that in any way, which suggested this effect was achieved with either a dev menu or cheats.
In the wake of Cyberleek’s initial leaks, Take-Two issued subpoenas to the likes of Discord as part of its search for the person or group of people responsible. It remains unclear how the gameplay footage, any potential build of the game it was taken from, or this latest Xbox build, escaped the confines of Rockstar's infamous tight security.
In August, Rockstar addressed the GTA 6 leaks , describing the situation as "heartbreaking" for its development team and "unfortunate" for fans. At the time, the developer acknowledged that its intended experience for players "may now be impacted by some spoilers," but reiterated GTA 6's previously-confirmed launch date of November 19.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.content_orig:
The United States military on Friday announced it had fired at a ship in the Gulf of Oman that it said was violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports .
A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" in the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer, US Central Command (CENTCOM), said, adding that it "continues to strictly enforce the [US] blockade."
CENTCOM oversees US forces in the Middle East.
The statement said that "the ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled" and stressed that "the civilian crew was unharmed."
It said that the ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas.
The US blockade has disabled six ships and redirected 158 others.
Washington launched its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July following the collapse of an agreement with Tehran.
The war broke out in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran , which prompted Tehran to impose its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz .
Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a Thursday drone strike killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti military site.
A Kuwaiti citizen and a Pakistani citizen were also injured and hospitalized in the attack.
Iran has denied responsibility for the strike.

Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Al-Mashaan condemned the "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defense.
The two technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, a subsidiary of the German defense firm Rheinmetall .
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, calling on "all parties to exercise restraint."
Guterres is "deeply concerned by the continued escalation in the region," according to his spokesman, Stephane Dujarric. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues.
Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”.
Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.
Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.”
He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.
“We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.”
The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island’s main highways, forcing its closure.
Organisers estimated that some 8,000 people took part, according to local media.
Many in the crowd waved or wore the Puerto Rican flag. Some chose the flag from before the island became a US commonwealth in 1952, often a sign of cultural pride and sometimes of resistance.
“Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse,” said Veronica Ishtar, a visual arts student.
This week alone, she said the power in her neighbourhood went out 12 times.
In addition, monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18 percent, with the new rate per kilowatt-hour far surpassing the average for residential customers on the US mainland, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Some protesters blamed Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court approved a move to cancel the government’s contract with Luma on Wednesday, but many now worry about what comes next.
Puerto Rico’s Association of Industries said the cancellation could discourage private investment and jeopardise existing projects as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
The leaders of several groups that organised the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.
“We must begin to channel the rage,” said Hernaliz Vazquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. “We must begin to organise the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do.”

articles.title_orig: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.title_zh: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.content_orig:
European leaders failed to break a deadlock over the EU's next long-term budget on Thursday, leaving negotiators under pressure to meet their year-end target before a busy 2027 election cycle adds further complications.
National leaders are divided over the European Union's next long-term budget, which sets spending priorities and limits from 2028 to 2034. It requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states to pass, as well as a majority vote in favor from members of the European Parliament.
Representatives from EU member states met on Wednesday and Thursday to discuss the latest budget proposal from European Council President António Costa, which amounts to a spending plan worth 1.58 trillion euros ($1.73 trillion). It marks a downward revision of around 10% from the original proposals for the bloc's long-term budget — known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF.
The EU's budget negotiations come against a backdrop of surging government borrowing costs, spiraling inflation and sluggish growth across much of the continent, as well as concerns about rising budget deficits in various EU countries.
Failure to meet the year-end deadline for the budget to be agreed risks deepening the political deadlock at the center of the ongoing talks.
At a summit in Brussels Thursday, budget talks went on for 12 hours, according to a BBC report — with some participants said to have walked out of the meeting as conflicts emerged around spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
A spokesperson for the European Commission was not available to comment on Thursday's talks.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters on Thursday evening that the talks had brought "new movement" towards reducing the overall size of the budget, adding that leaders would reconvene in mid-December to resume talks.
But he also said: "The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
Merz, alongside the leaders of Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria, Finland and Sweden, said in September that the original 2-trillion-euro proposal would need to be reduced by "several hundred billion euros."
"We must make choices," they said in a letter addressed to Costa and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin, pointing out that their six countries finance almost 40% of all contributions to the budget.
They called for funding to be focused on defense spending, competitiveness and innovation and "the fight against irregular migration."
Costa labeled the revised budget plans "realistic" when he presented them last week, noting that despite the 10.2% reduction in spending the proposals still represented a 120% jump in competitiveness funding and a 232% upswing for defense compared to the current budget.
"We didn't reach an agreement," he said in a statement after Thursday's meeting. "Regarding the global volume of the budget, some member states asked for further reductions, most opposed further cuts. And some even proposed to reverse some cuts."
Some European parliamentarians also appeared unconvinced by the new proposals.
"Parliament is consistent and proposes more investments, [the] Council is inconsistent and proposes cuts," Romanian MEP Siegfried Mureşan said on Wednesday.
"When the Council finally reaches a position, that's when negotiations will start, not when they end. As prime ministers cannot dictate to national parliaments, prime ministers also cannot dictate to the European Parliament to adopt a budget that is too small, and which does not equip Europe for the future."
Elections are set to go ahead in key EU economies including Spain, Poland and Italy over the next 12 months, while France's spring presidential election is at the forefront of regional leaders' minds.
Current front-runner for the French presidency, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, has previously called for the country to leave the EU and to cut its contributions to the bloc's budget.
Incumbent French President Emmanuel Macron stressed on Thursday that he had limited time left to have his say on EU spending.
"After 31 December, I will no longer be in a position, politically or democratically, to reopen discussions on the budget and bring them to a conclusion, as we will be ​entering a period far too close to the presidential election in France," he told reporters after the talks, according to French publication France 24 .
France, the EU's second-biggest economy after Germany, is being tasked with drastically cutting spending to bring its 5.1% national deficit closer to an EU guideline of 3%, while reeling from months of mass protests, riots and strikes over education funding and a cost-of-living crisis.

articles.title_orig: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
articles.title_zh: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
articles.content_orig:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.
The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
