articles.title_orig: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
articles.title_zh: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
articles.content_orig:
Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump.
It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era.
The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País ' s final polling averages . A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO.
It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year.
Despite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises.
Inflation soared to 4.9% in the year to October, above a euro zone average of 4%. November's flash estimate published Friday showed Spanish inflation cooling to 4.1%, still well above the 2.3% reading at the start of the year. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing one of the country's two most important issues.
Home purchase prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat . In 2025, house prices rose nearly three times as fast as household incomes, the European Commission said.
Nationwide protests began after an 87-year-old woman died two weeks after being evicted from her Madrid apartment in September.
Sánchez called the snap election after lawmakers rejected two government decrees designed to broaden housing protections, including limiting rent increases and blocking certain evictions and automatic lease renewals. Congress later ratified a revised version of one decree, limiting rent increases and evictions in some circumstances.
Sánchez has made a name for himself internationally after clashing with Trump over NATO spending, the war in Gaza and Spain's refusal to let U.S. forces use its bases for operations against Iran. Trump even threatened to cut off "all trade" with Spain during the dispute over the bases.
At a Nov. 21 rally in Tenerife, Sánchez asked: "What good has President Trump brought to the United States and, by extension, to the world?"
He has also told voters that the PP and Vox would roll back government cost-of-living assistance. Days before the election, Sánchez's government approved 1.21 billion euros ($1.33 billion) to extend public transport discounts through 2027 and approved a general pay increase of up to 4.5% for 2027.
But in a final pre-election survey for El Español on Nov. 23, 66% of respondents gave Sánchez a failing grade and 29.5% a passing one. His government has faced scrutiny over its handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis, two deadly train collisions this year and corruption cases involving people close to the prime minister.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the current favorite to replace Sánchez, has made alleged government corruption and inflation central to his campaign. At a Nov. 22 rally in Murcia, he said the government wanted voters to forget "that inflation is eating into your pay check, that you can't afford a home, that you're paying more than ever for everything."
The PP led the final El País polling average, published Nov. 24, with 31.4%, followed by Sánchez's Socialists at 29.1% and Vox at 17.9%. Several seat projections put the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. If Vox joins a government, it would be the first far-right party to do so since Spain returned to democracy after Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled for 40 years, died in 1975.
The PP wants to repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in designated high-pressure areas. It proposes speeding up construction permits and lowering taxes on first homes for buyers under 40. Vox also wants to repeal the housing law and would prioritize Spanish citizens for subsidized housing and public services.
Sánchez's Socialists want to extend renter protections and make at least a quarter of new homes public or permanently price-restricted. It would use proceeds from a bank levy to support housing, which it says will raise a further $1.5 billion. The PP has pledged to scrap this.
The PP also favors easing climate rules, extending the life of nuclear plants and replacing a decree that sets tight new renewable-power requirements on data centers with large new grid connections.
A PP-Vox coalition would have its tensions, with immigration likely to be a major pressure point as Vox has an increasingly hard line on deportation and the militarization of some borders. The parties clashed in regional governments over the distribution of unaccompanied migrant children, leading Vox to quit several coalitions in 2024.
Immigration has since gained more prominence amid the government's handling of reports that more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31.
"Immigration has played a significant role in supporting Spain's recent growth, a strong role for Vox could complicate the government's ability to sustain that," said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
The parties also differ on defense commitments: both support more investment, but neither has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defense. The PP pledges closer NATO cooperation, while Vox puts greater emphasis on border security.
The PP favors closer integration with the European Union, while Vox wants more independence from it. The success or failure of a PP-Vox partnership will also have wider lessons for Europe "where long-standing firewalls against far-right parties are coming under strain," added Middleton, pointing to the rise of Germany's AfD and the prospect of Marine Le Pen potentially winning next year's election in France.
A shift to the right could improve relations between the U.S. and Spain. Sánchez used his tenure to strengthen ties with Beijing, the country's largest goods trading partner outside the EU.
The U.S. remained Spain's largest source of foreign direct investment. Flows more than doubled to 11.6 billion euros in the 12 months through June 2026, from 5.1 billion euros in the previous 12 months, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Carla Hobbs, head of the European Council on Foreign Relations' Madrid office, expects a PP-led government to seek closer ties with Washington and bring its China policy more in line with the EU's. Vox could complicate that. The first test for Washington would be whether a new government changes Spain's position on defense spending or the use of its bases.

You can use the links below to jump directly to the section you're shopping for today.

articles.title_orig: A 60-Year-Old Who Bought 1,000 Micron Shares at $192 Just Watched Jim Cramer's Investing Club Call It 'Comically Cheap.' Here's What's Left of His $1 Million Gain - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: A 60-Year-Old Who Bought 1,000 Micron Shares at $192 Just Watched Jim Cramer's Investing Club Call It 'Comically Cheap.' Here's What's Left of His $1 Million Gain - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A 60-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) shares at $192.37 had a gain of about $1 million in June. At Friday’s close, $454,580 of it is left. On Wednesday, with the stock down as much as 13% on the day, Jim Cramer’s CNBC Investing Club looked at Micron’s price and wrote, "That is comically cheap."
He is an example I built on Nov. 5 to show the math, the night Micron fell 17% and took $138,840 from him in one session. I’ll add what that story left out: he retired this year and has $500,000 in other savings. His shares cost $192,370. They were worth $1,213,560 at the record close on June 25 and $646,950 on Friday, after Micron rose nearly 8% in a half-day session.
A stock at about 3 times next year’s expected earnings reads as a bargain, and the Club told its members to hold. It is also what a memory chip stock looks like when investors expect those earnings to fall, and Micron traded at about 5 times earnings in 2018 before a 54% drop.
The line came in the Club’s Wednesday afternoon note to members, written by Kevin Stankiewicz and Zev Fima. Micron "continues to trade as if memory is no longer a crucial component of the AI buildout," they wrote. "Nothing could be further from the truth."
Their math: Wall Street expects Micron to earn $175.22 a share in fiscal 2027, which runs through next summer, and $207.71 in fiscal 2028. At a stock price of $570, that is 3.25 times the first figure and 2.75 times the second. The Club’s reading is that the price "reflects tremendous skepticism" that Micron will hit those numbers. Its conclusion: "while the price action is gut-wrenching, the fundamentals argue in favor of staying the course."
Jim Cramer’s Charitable Trust, the portfolio the Club follows, owned Micron as of the Club’s Sept. 30 note, so the Club is describing its own position.
At Friday’s close of $646.95 the same math gives 3.7 times the fiscal 2027 estimate. For the retiree the estimate has a simpler meaning. Analysts expect Micron to earn $175.22 a share in a single year. He paid $192.37 for each share.
Each value is 1,000 shares at that day’s closing price.
This week the stake moved by $113,190, $77,910, $28,540 and $45,700 in four sessions. That is $265,340 of daily swings on shares that cost him $192,370. Measured from the record, $566,610 is gone, 55% of the gain he had in June.
Memory chips are a boom and bust business, and Micron’s price looks lowest against its earnings when those earnings are at their highest. On May 29, 2018, the stock closed at $62.62, about 5 times the $11.95 a share Micron earned in the fiscal year that ended that August. By Dec. 24 it closed at $29.02, down 54% in seven months. Two fiscal years later Micron earned $2.83 a share, 76% less. The low multiple in 2018 was a forecast, and the forecast was right.
Micron told investors on Sept. 30 to expect about $38.15 a share for its current quarter, 8 times the $4.78 it earned a year earlier. The doubt is about how long that lasts. Of 49 analysts in Alpha Vantage’s count, 45 rate the stock a buy. Their average target is about $1,530, more than double Friday’s close.
That story, "A 60-Year-Old Who Bought 1,000 Micron Shares at $192 Just Lost $138,840," suggested selling a third: 333 shares at $656.39, or $218,578. Six days later those shares were worth $51,585 more. On Nov. 20 they were worth $20,606 less. At Friday’s close the seller is $3,144 ahead, close to nothing on a stake this size.
Waiting did give him one thing. The stock was last near his price on Nov. 21, 2025, when it touched $192.59, so his one-year mark passed last weekend. A sale now is taxed as a long-term gain. On Nov. 5 it would have been taxed as ordinary income.
Micron is 56% of his $1,146,950. Across all U.S. households, stocks of every kind were a record 48.2% of financial assets in the second quarter, Federal Reserve data show, well above the 38.7% reached at the dot-com peak. He has more than that in one company. A 10% move in Micron changes his total savings by $64,695.
He has three honest answers.
Hold all 1,000. This is the Club’s answer. If Micron reaches the analysts’ average target, the stake is worth $1,529,690. If the stock repeats its 2018 fall from here, the stake is worth about $300,000 and the gain is $107,446.
Sell 333 shares. At Friday’s close that brings in $215,434. The gain on those shares is $151,375, and at the 15% federal long-term rate the tax is at most $22,706. He keeps $192,728, which is $358 more than he paid for all 1,000 shares. The 667 shares he still owns are worth $431,516, and Micron falls to 38% of his savings. If the analysts’ average target is right, those 667 shares alone are worth $1,020,303.
Set a line before two dates. The Club wrote that Micron could announce a share buyback as early as Dec. 9, and the next earnings report is expected on Dec. 17. He can decide this weekend what would make him sell the third: a company forecast below the $38.15 it gave in September, or a close under the Nov. 20 low of $594.51, which is 8% below Friday’s price. A rule written on a quiet weekend is easier to follow than one made at Monday’s open.
Each answer depends on what else he could own with the money, and that list is outside this story. Eric Bleeker runs a $1 million AI Investor Portfolio in The Daily Profit, our free weekday email, and an issue before Micron’s Dec. 17 report will say whether it holds Micron and how much sits in its largest position. Sign up free here and you also get our Top 10 Stocks to Buy Right Now report.
The retiree is an example, and his $500,000 of other savings is my assumption. The values use closing prices, which no real seller gets exactly. The tax figure assumes a taxable brokerage account and income that keeps him in the 15% bracket, which runs to $545,500 of taxable income for a single filer in 2026. State tax is extra. The earnings estimates are the consensus figures the Club quoted, and Micron has not confirmed the Dec. 17 date.
Cramer’s Club may be right that Micron is comically cheap, and the retiree can act without knowing. Selling a third returns every dollar he put in, after tax, and leaves 667 shares to find out.

Dutch authorities ​seized 26 critically endangered mud turtles at Amsterdam ’s Schiphol airport last week, the Dutch Food and Consumer ⁠Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday.
The Vallarta turtles were brought in from Mexico, where a mere 300 of them are believed to remain in the wild.
Vallarta turtles are one of the world’s smallest turtle species, and have been linked with illegal trade due to their considerable financial value.
According to the NVWA, the turtles were hidden in the checked baggage of ​a ⁠man who was travelling ‌to Hong Kong .
The man was subsequently arrested, while further investigations are ongoing.
Most of the turtles were packed inside of a box alongside a toy car, while a handful of others were placed inside of a sealed sock.
The turtles had been wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
All of the turtles survived and were taken to a specialist animal rescue centre, the NVWA said.
According to the US-based ⁠ Center for Biological Diversity , Vallarta mud turtles are sold for large sums in China .
“Vallarta mud turtles sell for up to $30,000 each in China, providing a major financial incentive that drives illegal trade,” it said in a statement last month, calling on ‌the Mexican ​government to do ‌more to protect the ​animals.
“Experts believe wildlife authorities only seize a small portion of illegal traded wildlife.”
A similar incident occurred in December 2025 at Los Angeles International Airport , the Center said, where “approximately 20 Vallarta mud turtles bound for Asia” were seized.
Based on US Fish and Wildlife Service data, Tara Easter, a University of Michigan doctoral candidate who has studied the trade, previously estimated the commercial export trade for mud turtles in the United States increased from 1,844 in 1999 to nearly 40,000 in 2017.

articles.title_orig: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.title_zh: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.content_orig:
Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.
The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.
The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.
And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable â and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Psychologist Sebastian LundstrÃ¶m runs the clinic, which operates one day a month
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.
This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.
Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (Â£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.
But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.
Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.
The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian LundstrÃ¶m, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.
LundstrÃ¶m says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism SkÃ¥ne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.
Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
LundstrÃ¶m says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.
Before opening the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.
During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to LundstrÃ¶m, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

MANILA — Harassing ships in the South China Sea. Weaponizing its virtual monopoly on critical rare earth minerals . Keeping the world guessing about its advances in artificial intelligence .
As China flexes its economic and military muscle, some of Washington’s closest allies are preparing to press President Trump to take a harder line as he visits the region this week , urging a united front against Beijing’s growing assertiveness in a part of the world where American influence once went largely unchallenged.
Within his own administration, several officials echoed calls on the president to assume a tougher stance ahead of his arrival.
“We do think it’s time for China to step up to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” one senior administration official said, accusing Beijing of pursuing “opaque” defensive programs with potentially world-altering consequences, from a rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal to artificial intelligence capabilities exceeding human control.
Trump will gather in Manila with leaders from powerful democracies across the Indo-Pacific, and meet with other regional allies from Southeast Asia.
Trump will receive a formal banquet welcome from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. when he arrives in the Philippines on Tuesday, just two months after the Chinese Coast Guard rammed a Philippine vessel tending to fishermen off Palawan’s coast. He plans to fly to China from there on Wednesday afternoon.
Manila’s famously congested streets were unusually quiet after the government declared an extended holiday to clear traffic for the international summit. Banners marking the gathering hung across the capital, lending the city a festive air as it prepared to host world leaders.
The Quad — composed of India, Japan, Australia and the United States, four influential regional democracies — will meet for the first time in two years in Manila, where Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
Trump will meet with the group first thing upon his arrival  Tuesday before signing a trade agreement with Thailand. That night, the president will attend a gala dinner with members of the Assn. of Southeast Asian Nations, known as ASEAN.
Marcos will host Trump for a state visit on Wednesday morning before the president flies to Shenzhen , a city in southern China referred to locally as its Silicon Valley.
Without naming China explicitly, foreign ministers of the Quad laid out the stakes for the meeting in a statement after huddling in October, expressing “grave concerns regarding economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity to disrupt global supply chains in critical industries.”
Japan’s foreign ministry expressed hope the group would discuss the dangers posed by artificial intelligence, seeking to broaden the Quad’s role beyond maritime security to build a common front against China’s growing technological influence.
“Strategic circumstances in our region are deteriorating,” said Australia’s foreign minister, Penny Wong, at the time, adding: “The region is facing acute economic stress. We know the world is more unpredictable, we know economic volatility is increasing.”
Indian officials hope to focus the meeting on reducing global dependence on China’s near-total monopoly on heavy rare earths, after signing an agreement with Washington in May to develop alternative supply chains spanning mining, processing and recycling.
The meeting itself will be serve as a message to China ahead of Trump’s bilateral meeting with Xi and, afterward, an extraordinary trilateral gathering with the Chinese leader and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
So, too, will Trump’s visit to a country that has served as a critical U.S. military ally in the postwar order.
Despite Trump’s overtures to Xi, the president has increased the size and scope of its military exercises with the Philippines in his second term, incorporating regional allies, such as Japan, to take part in a collective defensive effort designed around potential Chinese ambitions.
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
Still, White House officials have said that Trump would enter his meetings in Manila with an “America first” agenda, forging “commercial deals and strategic investments” that reflect “more balanced and fair trade for American businesses, farmers and workers.” Trump’s tariff policies have been a constant source of tension between his administration and regional allies.
Marco Rubio, Trump’s secretary of State and national security advisor, has sought to strike a delicate diplomatic balance ahead of the meetings, tempering expectations that the Manila talks would center on containing China’s rise.
But he also acknowledged the primary source of regional anxieties.
“The Quad is not an anti-anybody. It’s not a format that exists to be against any country,” Rubio told reporters in October, when asked about China. “To the extent we express concern about things in the Quad, it’s concern about behaviors. It’s concern about activities.”
“Now, those activities or behaviors are coming repetitively from one country,” Rubio continued, adding: “That’s going to be obvious to everybody.”
As Trump left the White House Monday, he said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un while in China. Kim “may come” to Shenzhen but “that’s up to President Xi,” Trump told reporters, according to the Associated Press.
He also said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“We’ll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” Trump said. “Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers in the month. So we’ll be talking about that.”

articles.title_zh: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.title_zh: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.content_orig:
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
Shenzhen, a rich, buzzing city on the south-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ay

articles.title_orig: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.title_zh: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.content_orig:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.
One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.
"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.
Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.
"So, I believe that young must mobilise."
As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.

articles.title_orig: China’s Cabinet Stresses Market Support in Rare Midday Statement
articles.title_zh: China’s Cabinet Stresses Market Support in Rare Midday Statement
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Los Angeles schools block Google’s AI features, consider dropping tech giant’s products
articles.title_zh: Los Angeles schools block Google’s AI features, consider dropping tech giant’s products
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES -- School districts are taking steps to block Google's artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America's classrooms.
In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.
The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.
The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board's A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.
"It was the talk of the playground," Lee said.
Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America's classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google's suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.
But concerns about AI's impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country's two largest school districts — New York and LA — announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it's not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.
LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are "age-appropriate and safe." It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.
Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.
"We're thrilled LAUSD did this," said Lee. "AI is seeping into everything. It's dangerous. It's hurting learning. And it's a corporate overreach into public schools. It's Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone's consent."
Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.
Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cellphones and screentime and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.
The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That's when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and LA schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.
Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.
Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.
While the blog post does not explicitly say search can't be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: "Search and AI are deeply integrated." If schools ban AI, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."
The integration of AI in search isn't new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.
Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company's leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features "without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole."
"The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we're punishing schools for not using AI," the petition said. "Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products."
Google says it hears parents' and teachers' concerns about students using AI to "shortcut learning" and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want — the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024 — is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students' access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.
Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot "guided learning" tool that walks students "step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers."
"We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers," the company said in a statement.
Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.
LA schools had already disabled Google's AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district's chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.
"We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite," Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google's products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district's priorities.
"We have choices," Kelanic said. "We can change the default search engine literally overnight."

articles.title_orig: NBC pulls ‘indefensible’ anti-Israel ad that aired during ‘SNL’ special: ‘Carefully orchestrated lie’
articles.title_zh: NBC pulls ‘indefensible’ anti-Israel ad that aired during ‘SNL’ special: ‘Carefully orchestrated lie’
articles.content_orig:
The 30-second spot claimed Israel uses U.S. military aid to target children
Roberto Machado Noa/LightRocket via Getty Images
NBC logo at Universal Studios.
NBC aired an ad on Wednesday during the Thanksgiving special of “Saturday Night Live” encouraging viewers to oppose U.S. aid to Israel, claiming Israel uses such aid to target Palestinian children.
The 30-second spot, which aired nationally and was paid for by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project , depicted an American girl saving $400 for a new bike, before showing a girl in Gaza on crutches with one leg. A narrator says, “Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this.”
The ad directs viewers to IMEU Policy Project’s “No More for Israel” campaign site, which says, “The US government has sent Israel over $330 billion in inflation-adjusted dollars since 1948. That’s $400 every three seconds nonstop for nearly eighty years. Much of it with our tax dollars.”
The figure appears to be referencing high-end estimates of such assistance — the Congressional Research Service most recently estimated it was approximately $298 billion, inflation adjusted, between 1946 and 2024. It also obscures that almost all U.S. military assistance to Israel is now spent within the U.S and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has championed ending U.S. aid to Israel, including President Donald Trump’s announcement earlier this month that he had agreed with Netanyahu to wind down assistance by the end of the year.
Jewish leaders immediately condemned the decision by NBC to air the ad. Ted Deutch, CEO of the American Jewish Committee, noted that the spot did not reference Hamas or its Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, and called on NBC to “explain why and how an ad this one-sided and manipulative met its standards for what it will put on the air.”
Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said NBC’s decision to air the ad was “indefensible” and that there is “no rationale to justify fanning the flames” of rising antisemitism “with such a twisted narrative.”
William Daroff, CEO of the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, called NBC’s airing of the spot a “shanda.”
The National Jewish Advocacy Center sent a letter to Mark Marshall, chairman of global advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal, noting that NBC’s “own published standards required a factual basis for that claim before it reached the air” and requesting that the network provide such reasoning to the public.
The decision to air the ad was especially notable given that Brian Roberts, chairman and CEO of Comcast, NBCUniversal’s parent company, hails from a prominent Jewish family that has been publicly and financially supportive of Israel.
Following the Oct. 7 attacks, Roberts and Comcast President Mike Cavanagh sent a note to employees saying they were “horrified and deeply saddened by the brutal attack on Israel,” expressing solidarity with “the families who have lost their loved ones through unspeakable acts of terrorism and the devastation of war.” Comcast pledged $2 million to humanitarian aid efforts in Israel and around the region.
Daniel Lubetzky, the founder of KIND Snacks, focused his criticism on Semafor , the outlet which broke the story that IMEU Policy Project would be running the ad. He said the outlet “needs to be investigated for corruption. And for sure should not be treated as journalism,” following on his accusation last month that the outlet is compromising its journalistic independence through its financial ties to Qatar.
Deutch similarly called out Semafor for reporting on the ad “largely on the terms its sponsors wanted, with remarkably little scrutiny of what the ad leaves out.”

articles.title_orig: Earliest iron scale armor in China found near First Emperor’s tomb
articles.title_zh: Earliest iron scale armor in China found near First Emperor’s tomb
articles.content_orig:
Archaeologists working beside the mausoleum of China’s First Emperor have uncovered what appears to be the earliest complete suit of iron scale armor ever found in the country. A team from University College London and the Emperor Qin Shihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum reported the find in the journal Antiquity.
The armor came from tomb M1, the third of nine large tombs stretching west of the emperor’s main burial enclosure. Crews excavated the site from 2013 to 2023. The main chamber covers 1,900 square meters and sits 15.6 meters below ground. Inside, the team found two coffins, a four-wheeled wooden carriage and horse-and-chariot burials in side pits. No other Qin tomb dug so far is richer or better preserved. Nobody knows who lay there, but the person held high rank.
The iron scales sat in a heap on the south side of the chamber. The ceiling collapsed long ago, and the scales likely dropped from a shelf. Corrosion broke most of the metal into tiny pieces, yet the team still counted at least 200 larger fragments. They estimate the suit held 800 to 1,200 scales. A helmet would need only 80 to 90, and several suits would need far more, so the pile points to one body piece. Such a garment would weigh about 10 kilograms.
Most scales are small rectangles, roughly 33 by 29 millimeters and 1.5 millimeters thick, with 10 tiny holes for lacing. A heavier type has 11 holes, and a few fish-scale shapes turned up too. Mapping with micro X-ray fluorescence found traces of cinnabar, a red mercury pigment, on nearly every scale tested. Some pieces carry flakes of a black coating, likely lacquer. The team found no gold or silver plating. A Han Dynasty iron suit from Linzi, which held 2,142 scales, was gilded.
Under a scanning electron microscope, five scales showed low-carbon steel, with 0.1 to 0.4 percent carbon. Grains measured 10 to 20 microns across, a sign of heavy hammering. Slag was scarce. Smiths most likely started with cast iron, stripped out carbon in a process called fining, and forged the result into thin sheets. This matches what researchers know about Qin iron work. The small sample leaves room for another route, direct smelting of solid iron.
The mausoleum holds other armor made of different materials. The Terracotta Army wears clay armor, and the brown scales seem to copy leather. Smaller gray scales on some higher-ranking figures might stand in for iron. In pit K9801, crews dug only about 1 percent of the area and pulled out 87 stone corselets and 43 stone helmets. Their scales look much like the M1 scales and were laced with flat copper wire.
Qin law texts written on bamboo slips hint at the cost. A penalty of making one set of scale armor equaled 168 to 224 days of labor. The authors say an iron suit, with smaller scales and finer lacing, might have kept a small workshop busy for a year or more.
One puzzle remains. Iron swords also lay in tomb M1, yet the mausoleum holds tens of thousands of bronze weapons. Some scholars think the bronze was symbolic. Old reign dates on weapons from Pit 1 suggest the army drew on aging stock. The authors don’t settle the debate. They plan to study more iron tools and weapons from the complex.

articles.title_orig: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3?
articles.title_zh: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3?
articles.content_orig:
By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:28PM EST
10 stocks we like better ›
Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia ( NVDA +0.80% ) , but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.
Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.
On Dec. 1, Huang will testify before the U.S. House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committee, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter will also testify before the same committees on Dec. 2. Both hearings will be private, with transcripts not expected to be published publicly for some time.
But on Dec. 3, Huang will testify at a live hearing before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, an event that will be closely monitored by all investors. Should investors buy Nvidia stock before these hearings?
While President Donald Trump has come out in support of Huang and claims to have played a role in his reinstatement, the hearings will help reveal how other lawmakers feel about Huang and what's going on with Nvidia.
"The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of issues that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Yorkville Ives analyst and Managing Partner Dan Ives wrote in a recent research note, according to Business Insider. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC."
Huang's reinstatement as CEO led to a swift surge in the stock, but since then, shares have been pressured by lingering investor concerns about the company.
Multiple reports suggest that a woman Huang had an affair with, named Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center company MegaSpeed, may have facilitated a network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26
Investors are trying to understand how much prior demand for Nvidia's chips, if any, may have been driven by similar sources. Since the scandal came to light, the U.S. Commerce Department has moved to close loopholes and tighten export controls that may have allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely.
The Commerce Department is now also requiring companies in select countries, such as Singapore and Indonesia, to obtain a license before transferring or reexporting advanced chips from U.S. companies.
In his note, Ives said he believes the impact on revenue resulting from such export controls is "a containable 15% to 20% at most." Still, that's a significant amount, and while some of it is priced in, Nvidia stock could certainly face more pressure if it believed future demand wouldn't be as strong.
Given that Wall Street analysts like Ives are already contemplating what would happen to Nvidia's revenue if increased export restrictions lower demand, or some sources of demand abroad are closed off, it's clear the market is pricing in at least some of the potential impact.
Still, Wall Street consensus estimates expect Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share on an adjusted basis for its fiscal year 2028 ending in late January 2028. That means Nvidia trades at just 9x forward earnings , so the valuation is attractive.
But as we've seen through this whole debacle, things can change in a hurry, so I would never tell investors to buy a stock based on a near-term event like a Congressional hearing.
With Nvidia trading at a cheap level, I think investors can purchase a position to hold long term. But I do not believe that the majority of a traditional stock portfolio should be concentrated in Nvidia or AI stocks, as much uncertainty remains.

articles.title_zh: U.S. Strikes Vessel Attempting Blockade Run Near Iran
articles.content_orig:
The military alleged the commercial vessel had "precision munitions."
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
U.S. Central Command said it disabled a commercial vessel with "precision munitions" in the Gulf of Oman Thursday after the ship allegedly tried to run the U.S. Naval blockade against Iran.
The U.S. military struck the ship's stern, disabling propulsion of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer shortly after it left an Iranian port, according to CENTCOM.
The military said that the ship's civilian crew was unharmed.
Gen. Sardar Shekarchi, spokesperson of Iran's armed forces, denies that Iran carried out a drone attack on Kuwait.
According to Iran's official state news agency IRNA, Shekarchi "categorically and completely" rejected claims by the Kuwaiti military that Iranian forces attacked vital Kuwaiti sites.
"No military or offensive operations have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region," Shekarchi said, according to IRNA.
"Given the history of hostile actions -- including the use of 'false flag' tactics and regional adventurism by the Zionist regime and U.S. forces -- these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region," Shekarchi said.
Kuwaiti authorities have blamed Iran for the attack that killed two Italian nationals and injured one Kuwaiti and one Pakistani national.
-ABC News' Jamie Dorrington
The two Italian nationals injured in Thursday's Iranian drone attack in Kuwait have died, a spokesperson for Kuwait's Ministry of Defense said in a statement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences to the victim's families in a post on X.
"On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," Meloni said.
The Kuwait Army on Thursday reported that four people were injured by falling shrapnel after an Iranian drone attack targeted "a vital site" in the Gulf state.
The army said in a post to X that Kuwaiti forces "dealt with" the incoming drones. "Material damage also occurred," the statement added.
Those injured were two Italian nationals, one Pakistani national and one Kuwaiti national, the army said.
